paragraphs: This paper develops statistical tests for whether two multivariate quantities are independent. Its starting point is a general equivalence: independence can be assessed through cross-covariances among interaction coefficients built from binary expansions. The result applies across broad sample spaces, giving the approach a foundation beyond representations defined by kernels.

The difficulty is that the number of possible interactions grows exponentially. Directly constructing and checking them would be impractical. The authors reformulate the tests as U-statistics and derive an explicit kernel representation for efficient computation. They also exploit the multiple scales in binary expansions, selectively cutting off higher-order interactions to adapt to dependence patterns that are unknown beforehand.

Their adaptive aggregation method, wa-dCoBET, combines a basic binary-expansion covariance test with a version based on distance measures. In simulations and a real-data application, it matches or exceeds HSIC and distance covariance, especially for higher-dimensional and non-monotone relationships. Accurate type I error control means these detection gains are accompanied by appropriate control of false independence rejections in the reported evaluations.
icml-2026-adaptive-multiscale-binary-exp.tldr: Adaptive binary-expansion tests detect complex dependence efficiently while maintaining accurate false-positive control in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Models for graphs and point clouds often accept inputs of many different sizes. Traditional universality results, however, usually concern approximating functions on compact domains with a fixed input size. This paper asks how to formulate an analogous guarantee for a single model family operating across growing input sizes.

The authors connect a sequence of functions on finite inputs to one uniquely identified function on an infinite-dimensional limit space. That space contains inputs of every finite size together with their limits. Using input symmetries and relationships across sizes, they define a natural topology and identify rich families of compact sets on which universality can be established.

This construction makes expressive capacity across sizes a precise mathematical question. Applying it, the authors show that several existing architectures fail to be universal in this framework and propose simple modifications that restore universality. The contribution therefore combines a way to state the approximation problem with architectural consequences: supporting variable-sized inputs alone does not settle whether a model has the desired approximation power.
icml-2026-any-dimensional-invariant-univ.tldr: A limit-space framework defines universality across input sizes and exposes architectural gaps that simple modifications can repair.

paragraphs: Short text clustering groups brief texts by meaning without relying on supplied class labels. Optimal Transport methods can support this process by assigning temporary labels that subsequently guide model learning. The paper identifies a weakness in existing approaches: they may give different labels to texts with similar meanings, creating misleading supervision.

The proposed framework adds an instance-level attention mechanism that estimates semantic relationships between individual texts. These relationships enter the Optimal Transport formulation, allowing assignments to account for neighboring samples. The resulting labels reflect both the global relationship between samples and clusters and the local consistency between semantically related texts.

The model then learns from these jointly informed labels. This matters because errors in temporary assignments can influence the clusters learned afterward; improving consistency addresses that problem at the point where supervision is generated. Extensive experiments report performance above state-of-the-art methods. The stated finding supports combining global assignment structure with sample-to-sample semantic information as an effective approach to short text clustering.
icml-2026-beyond-looking-up-try-looking-.tldr: Adding semantic neighborhood information to Optimal Transport produces more reliable temporary labels for short text clustering.

paragraphs: Direct Preference Optimization offers a simpler route to preference-based training than Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. This paper argues that their theoretical equivalence depends on an implicit condition: the RLHF-optimal policy must favor the responses humans prefer. The authors prove that the equivalence is conditional and characterize situations where this assumption fails.

Under those failures, improving the DPO objective can mean improving a response's relative advantage over a reference policy without achieving absolute agreement with human preferences. Consequently, a policy can lower its DPO loss while still favoring dispreferred responses. A geometric analysis explains this through margin ranking whose targets can be negative, and the theory identifies an undesirable solution space.

The authors introduce Constrained Preference Optimization, which adds alignment constraints to RLHF, and establish provable alignment for their formulation. Experiments on standard benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance. The central implication is that preference-training loss and actual preference ordering can come apart; the paper identifies when existing guarantees apply and provides a constrained approach to address the analyzed failure.
icml-2026-conditional-equivalence-of-dpo.tldr: DPO's equivalence to RLHF depends on a preference-ordering assumption, motivating a constrained method with provable alignment.

paragraphs: Intracranial sEEG recordings capture neural activity with precise timing, but clinical constraints leave electrodes sparsely and irregularly distributed. EpiTwin reconstructs signals at unmonitored locations, potentially extending recording coverage without more implants. The paper targets two weaknesses in existing reconstruction methods: incomplete use of spatial information and predictions that smooth away meaningful signal variation.

Its spatial graph transformer combines three mechanisms. A positional encoding gives electrode contacts identities based on coordinates, graph connections, and anatomical information. Attention incorporates both physical distance and functional similarity inferred from data. Adversarial refinement with a multi-scale discriminator then discourages excessively smoothed reconstructions, complementing the model's spatial and functional reasoning.

On real clinical sEEG data, EpiTwin consistently reduces reconstruction error when electrode series are masked. The abstract reports a 16.8% relative RMSE reduction in its comparison with recent foundation models such as LaBraM. It also reports less spectral over-smoothing and improved fidelity, indicating gains in preserving signal characteristics alongside reductions in aggregate reconstruction error.
icml-2026-epitwin-spatiotemporal-graph-t.tldr: EpiTwin uses spatial, anatomical, and functional relationships to reconstruct missing sEEG signals with lower error and less over-smoothing.

paragraphs: Hypergraphs represent relationships involving groups of nodes. Contrastive learning on these structures often assumes that nodes sharing a hyperedge have similar meanings. This paper addresses cases where that assumption fails: information exchange can contaminate node features, while contrastive training can incorrectly encourage unlike nodes to align.

H²CL estimates the heterogeneity of each node–hyperedge interaction from input features. It uses those estimates to selectively mask highly heterogeneous connections when constructing training views. Its encoder also adjusts information flow in both directions, from nodes to hyperedges and back again, emphasizing more homogeneous signals and reducing the influence of heterogeneous noise.

A theoretical analysis connects the encoder to a coordinate descent step that minimizes a heterogeneity-weighted Dirichlet energy, providing an optimization interpretation of the propagation mechanism. Experiments on standard benchmarks and larger hypergraphs find competitive or superior performance against recent methods, robustness to structural noise, and learned weights that reduce heterogeneity during message passing. Together, these findings support accounting for differences within groups throughout both view construction and representation learning.
icml-2026-h-2-cl-heterogeneity-aware-hyp.tldr: H²CL improves hypergraph representations by detecting heterogeneous connections and adjusting both training views and information flow.

paragraphs: Language-model multi-agent systems must decide both how agents perform their roles and how they communicate. HieraMAS addresses these decisions together. It replaces the assumption that each role belongs to one indivisible agent with a supernode: several different language models contribute proposals that are combined through synthesis.

Optimizing this hierarchy creates a credit-assignment problem. Strong underlying models can produce good final results even when the surrounding configuration is suboptimal, potentially rewarding the wrong design choices. HieraMAS uses a two-stage algorithm: multi-level reward attribution provides feedback at both the node and whole-system levels, while graph classification selects communication structures as complete configurations.

Considering the topology as a whole allows the optimization to assess the arrangement of communication links together instead of making isolated decisions about each link. On reasoning and coding benchmarks, the framework significantly outperforms existing methods and achieves better cost-performance trade-offs. These results support coordinating the mixture within each role with the communication structure between roles when designing collaborative language-model systems.
icml-2026-hieramas-optimizing-intra-node.tldr: HieraMAS jointly organizes model mixtures within agent roles and communication between roles to improve performance and cost trade-offs.

paragraphs: Transformer feedforward layers store linguistic and factual knowledge in their parameters, while contextual events are available through the key–value cache. This paper explores integrating these forms of memory. It shows that the same group of feedforward parameters can hold both general knowledge and episodic information that can be retrieved without explicitly attending to the corresponding cache.

The proposed Hypermem system uses a hypernetwork to recurrently convert contexts into targeted changes to feedforward parameters. The hypernetwork is post-trained using continuation and random-access associative memory objectives. Once trained, it generates parameter updates from context without requiring test-time training, making the conversion of contextual information into parameter memory part of the learned mechanism.

Experiments cover memory retrieval, long-context question answering, and personalization. The method outperforms related approaches, including MemoryLLM and generative adapter, and establishes a reported state of the art among hypernetwork-based memory mechanisms. The findings suggest that directly connecting incoming information to parameter updates is a viable route toward more flexible and persistent model memory.
icml-2026-integrated-episodic-and-semant.tldr: Hypermem converts context into feedforward parameter updates, integrating episodic and semantic memory without test-time training.

paragraphs: Recovering full-body motion from signals recorded by a head-mounted device requires both plausible overall movement and accurate individual joints. The paper argues that diffusion methods focused on matching global motion distributions can still make local reconstruction errors. MotionGRPO adds reinforcement-learning post-training to give the diffusion process more detailed feedback.

The method treats diffusion sampling as a sequence of decisions and optimizes it with Group Relative Policy Optimization. Its reward combines a learned conditional perceptual model for overall visual plausibility with explicit constraints for joint precision. These components provide guidance at complementary levels, connecting whole-body appearance with the accuracy of particular joints.

The authors identify limited diversity among samples within a group as a cause of vanishing optimization gradients in this setting. They introduce noise injection to increase sample variance and stabilize learning. Extensive experiments report state-of-the-art performance and superior visual fidelity. The contribution therefore links a motion-specific reward design with a remedy for the weak learning signals that arise when grouped diffusion outputs are too similar.
icml-2026-motiongrpo-overcoming-low-intr.tldr: MotionGRPO improves body-motion reconstruction with detailed rewards and noise injection that strengthens learning from grouped diffusion samples.

paragraphs: Protein design often involves several functional goals that can compete with one another. Adjusting generation at test time offers a way to respond to changing goals without expensive retraining. This paper identifies three difficulties with existing diffusion approaches: repeating past errors, relying too heavily on successes for feedback, and handling conflicting objectives.

MoMST introduces a memory bank that extracts reusable reasoning experience from previous design iterations. It then compares successful and failed cases to derive relative preference signals at the residue level. This gives the generation process more detailed guidance than a single overall success signal and allows unsuccessful attempts to contribute information to subsequent designs.

An inference-time Pareto alignment strategy addresses conflicts between functional objectives. Together, the memory, comparative feedback, and alignment mechanism are intended to make test-time search more informed and balanced. Evaluations on both single-objective and complex multi-objective tasks report strong performance. The stated results support combining experience from prior attempts with residue-level guidance when adapting diffusion-based protein generation to changing design goals.
icml-2026-multi-objective-protein-design.tldr: MoMST guides protein diffusion at test time using remembered experience, successful and failed designs, and explicit management of competing objectives.

paragraphs: In multi-label text classification, frequent labels can dominate learning while rare labels receive less effective attention. This paper argues that scarcity alone does not explain the problem. Frequent labels can form dominant coalitions through misleading co-occurrences, taking over shared representations and gradient allocation while rare labels are learned through fragile shortcuts.

NBCG treats label groups as participants in a cooperative bargaining process. It first uses Neural Structural Equation Models to learn directed dependencies between labels. Those dependencies define causally coherent coalitions and coalition-specific communication masks, giving the groups a structured basis rather than forming them through arbitrary partitions.

Training then optimizes a Nash bargaining objective that compares each coalition's utility with an adaptive disagreement point. This provides a mechanism for allocating learning credit: underserved groups receive greater priority while the formulation maintains a Pareto-efficient trade-off among participants. The contribution is a reorganization of the learning problem around relationships and competition between label groups, addressing how optimization distributes attention beyond simply changing sample frequencies or assigning fixed weights.
icml-2026-nbcg-nash-bargained-causal-gam.tldr: NBCG organizes labels into learned dependency-based coalitions and uses Nash bargaining to prioritize underserved groups during training.

paragraphs: Language agents can improve answers by reflecting on previous attempts, but repeated reflections may say much the same thing. The paper reports a strong positive correlation between reflective diversity and task success. This observation motivates a memory mechanism designed to supply more varied reflection signals during iterative problem solving.

ParamMem stores reflection patterns drawn from multiple samples in model parameters. Temperature-controlled sampling then produces diverse reflections from this learned memory. The broader ParamAgent framework combines that parametric module with episodic memory and cross-sample memory, bringing learned patterns together with other sources of experience available to the agent.

Experiments on code generation, mathematical reasoning, and multi-hop question answering show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. Further analysis reports sample efficiency, transfer from weaker to stronger models, and self-improvement without a stronger external model. These findings support parametric reflective memory as a useful component for agents. The initial diversity finding remains a correlation, while the framework's reported task gains provide separate empirical evidence for the proposed design.
icml-2026-parammem-augmenting-language-a.tldr: ParamMem learns reusable reflection patterns in model parameters to help agents generate more diverse reflections and improve task performance.

paragraphs: Static benchmarks provide a limited view of how much knowledge can be extracted from a language model. This paper introduces an interactive framework that adaptively explores model knowledge rather than relying only on a fixed question set. Four exploration policies probe information at different levels of detail.

Extracted material passes through three processing stages. Vector-based filtering removes strict duplicates, language-model adjudication resolves uncertain semantic overlap, and domain auditing retains relevant knowledge units. This pipeline makes the measurement sensitive to distinct, valid information rather than simply counting generated statements. Among the tested exploration strategies, Recursive Taxonomy is the most effective.

The experiments find that larger models consistently yield more recoverable knowledge. They also reveal a trade-off between initial accuracy and sustained extraction: specialized models start more accurately but degrade rapidly, while general-purpose models remain more stable over extended probing. Different model families exhibit measurable knowledge profiles associated with their training-data composition. Together, these results show why both exploration strategy and extraction duration matter when assessing a model's accessible knowledge.
icml-2026-probing-the-knowledge-boundary.tldr: Adaptive knowledge probing reveals differences in recoverable knowledge, sustained extraction, and domain profiles across language models.

paragraphs: Sequential jailbreaks use multiple conversational turns to move a language model toward unsafe compliance. Evaluations that record only the final outcome reveal little about how that transition occurs. This paper develops an interpretable behavioral framework to distinguish measurable mechanisms associated with vulnerability over an interaction.

The framework pairs a controlled elicitation task, the Contextual Iowa Gambling Task, with a Generalized Rescorla–Wagner model. Across a diverse collection of mainstream language models, the analysis links vulnerability to interactions among optimism-biased learning, amplified perception of rewards, and a tendency to repeat previous choices. Model scale alone does not explain the observed differences.

The authors also find that counterfactual feedback and rewards framed through concepts such as regret, authority, and threat substantially accelerate movement from refusal to compliance. These results provide cognitive profiles of observed model behavior, expanding evaluation beyond a single success or failure judgment. The contribution is an interpretable account of how interaction and feedback relate to unsafe behavior, connecting language-agent research with methods from human behavioral science.
icml-2026-profiling-the-irrational-agent.tldr: Cognitive modeling links sequential jailbreak vulnerability to interacting behavioral factors and feedback effects that model size alone does not explain.

paragraphs: Multimodal diffusion transformers exchange information between text and image branches while generating images. This paper identifies a problem inside the text branch: as representations move through deeper layers, they progressively lose semantic information from the prompt. The authors examine this forgetting by probing linguistic attributes across layers in SD3, SD3.5, and FLUX.1.

Their remedy, prompt reinjection, brings representations from early text layers back into later layers. The approach requires no training. Its motivation follows directly from the observation that earlier representations preserve prompt information that becomes less available deeper in the network; reintroducing that information aims to maintain guidance during generation.

Experiments on GenEval, DPG, and T2I-CompBench++ report consistent improvements in instruction following. Metrics for preference, aesthetics, and overall text–image generation quality also improve. These findings indicate that maintaining the prompt's meaning within the model can benefit both adherence to textual requests and measured image quality. The method targets the internal persistence of prompt information through depth rather than requiring a newly trained generator.
icml-2026-prompt-reinjection-alleviating.tldr: Reintroducing early prompt representations into later diffusion-transformer layers improves instruction following without additional training.

paragraphs: Proactive language agents need to plan, ask questions, and interact across multiple turns. This creates a practical trade-off: too little initiative can leave user intentions poorly understood, while excessive requests for feedback can burden users. The paper develops Behavioral Agentic Optimization, or BAO, to train agents around both task performance and interaction quality.

BAO combines two parts within an agentic reinforcement-learning framework. Behavior enhancement develops proactive reasoning and information gathering. Behavior regularization discourages inefficient or redundant interactions and brings behavior closer to user expectations. Together, these mechanisms seek to improve the usefulness of an agent's initiative while controlling unnecessary demands on the user.

On multiple tasks from the UserRL benchmark suite, BAO substantially outperforms reinforcement-learning baselines under controlled comparisons. It also achieves performance comparable to, or better than, frontier language-model agents in the reported evaluations. The findings support explicitly training the balance between productive information gathering and interaction restraint, rather than treating successful task completion as the only relevant aspect of multi-turn behavior.
icml-2026-pushing-forward-pareto-frontie.tldr: BAO trains proactive agents to gather useful information while suppressing redundant interactions, improving reported task and engagement trade-offs.

paragraphs: Return-conditioned sequence models use a requested future return as an input for selecting behavior. Yet supplying a larger number does not by itself establish that the resulting policy will perform better. Q-ALIGN DT connects this control input to the policy's expected performance using a Q function.

The framework guides the sequence model so that the value of its output policy agrees with the requested return-to-go. It also fine-tunes the Q function together with the sequence model through return perturbation. This dense guidance is designed to produce an ordered family of behaviors, with higher requested returns corresponding consistently to trajectories with higher expected returns.

The theoretical analysis shows efficient learning of the desired policy and a near-optimal output when the requested return is sufficiently high. Experiments across D4RL report improved controllability and performance. The learned policy family also generalizes to velocity-tracking tasks where prior approaches fail. The contribution is therefore both performance-oriented and behavioral: the conditioning number gains a more precise relationship to what the model actually does.
icml-2026-return-to-go-is-more-than-a-nu.tldr: Q-ALIGN DT aligns requested returns with policy values, improving control and supporting near-optimal behavior when the requested return is sufficiently high.

paragraphs: Diffusion transformers are powerful image generators, but their computational demands complicate deployment. RobuQ studies how to train them with very low numerical precision. The paper identifies activation quantization as the main obstacle in low-bit settings, because activations are sensitive to approximation and have complicated distributions.

The framework first establishes a baseline with ternary weights and four-bit activations. Its RobustQuantizer then applies a Hadamard transform to convert unknown per-token distributions into normal distributions. An activation-only mixed-precision pipeline keeps ternary weights throughout the network while assigning different activation precisions to different layers, addressing information bottlenecks where they occur.

Experiments on ImageNet-1K report state-of-the-art performance and, according to the authors, the first stable image generation with activations averaging two bits. The average is significant: the approach allocates precision across layers rather than requiring every layer to use exactly two bits. The findings support treating activation distribution and layer-specific precision as central design choices for pushing diffusion transformers into extremely low-bit operation.
icml-2026-robuq-pushing-dits-to-w1-58a2-.tldr: RobuQ combines activation distribution transforms and layer-specific precision to achieve stable image generation with ternary weights and average two-bit activations.

paragraphs: Multi-agent reinforcement learning systems often struggle to transfer collaboration skills to unfamiliar tasks. The paper argues that useful structural assumptions need an intermediate level of abstraction. Entity-level assumptions can miss collaboration patterns, while assumptions about entire tasks may not cover new situations adequately.

The proposed role-level approach represents collaboration through transferable roles. Its method, Gaussian-mixture-model-based Transferable Role discovery, builds a structured role space that encourages diverse assignments. Regularization separates the roles, and the learned role structure is then used to support generalization. The intended balance combines flexibility about individual entities with information about how agents work together.

Empirical results show better zero-shot and few-shot transfer to unseen tasks than state-of-the-art methods. Zero-shot transfer assesses behavior without adaptation examples for the new task, while few-shot transfer allows limited examples. The reported gains support roles as a useful organizing principle for reusable collaboration: they preserve patterns of joint behavior at a level broader than individual entities and less tied to a particular complete task.
icml-2026-role-level-inductive-bias-for-.tldr: Learning diverse, separated roles improves reported transfer of multi-agent collaboration to unseen tasks with little or no adaptation.

paragraphs: Neural Granger methods use neural networks to study temporal dependencies in complex systems. Although the networks can capture nonlinear dynamics, causal discovery often relies on simple local measures extracted from them. This paper argues that such measures can overlook global dependencies already represented by the learned model.

The authors recast Granger causality as feature attribution and introduce an Information-Theoretic Shapley value, Info-Shap, to measure global feature importance. They establish a theoretical equivalence between a zero Info-Shap value and Granger non-causality. This connects the proposed attribution measure directly to the temporal dependency criterion the method seeks to recover.

Building on that result, the paper introduces two regularizers intended to suppress spurious relationships and reduce overfitting. They can be incorporated into any differentiable neural network, making the approach independent of a particular predictive architecture. Experiments on synthetic and realistic datasets report robust recovery of underlying causal relationships. The contribution combines a theoretically grounded global importance measure with training tools for discovering structure in high-dimensional nonlinear time series.
icml-2026-shapley-regularized-neural-gra.tldr: Info-Shap connects global feature attribution to Granger non-causality and supports regularizers that improve temporal structure recovery.

paragraphs: Long reasoning outputs can contain substantial repetition or other material that adds little to answer correctness. Common length penalties pressure every token equally, which can remove useful reasoning along with redundancy. This paper studies how to target the specific segments responsible for inefficient reasoning instead.

The authors find that inefficiency concentrates in high-probability segments with low marginal utility. They derive a theoretical characterization of when a segment is suboptimal under an objective that trades off correctness against length. SLAT uses this criterion within reinforcement learning to selectively discourage redundant segments, making compression sensitive to their contribution rather than merely their size.

On standard benchmarks, SLAT achieves a better reported accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier and reduces reasoning length by 50% relative to uncompressed baselines while retaining competitive accuracy. Competitive accuracy does not imply identical accuracy in every case; the finding concerns an improved overall trade-off. The results support analyzing reasoning at the segment level when training models to spend fewer tokens on material with limited value.
icml-2026-slat-segment-level-adaptive-tr.tldr: SLAT selectively discourages low-value reasoning segments, cutting reported reasoning length by 50% while maintaining competitive accuracy.

paragraphs: Flow matching learns velocities that move samples from a prior distribution toward data. This paper examines variance in the single-sample conditional velocities used as training targets. It identifies a difficult, high-variance region near the prior and a lower-variance region near the data, where conditional and marginal velocities nearly agree.

Stable Velocity uses this distinction for both training and generation. Stable Velocity Matching introduces an unbiased objective that reduces target variance. Variance-Aware Representation Alignment strengthens auxiliary supervision adaptively in the low-variance region. For inference, the authors derive closed-form simplifications of dynamics in that region and use them in a sampling method requiring no fine-tuning.

Experiments include ImageNet at 256-by-256 resolution and large pretrained image and video generators, including SD3.5, Flux, Qwen-Image, and Wan2.2. They show consistent training-efficiency improvements and more than twice as fast sampling within the low-variance region without degrading sample quality. That speed claim is explicitly regional; the contribution is to exploit different variance regimes rather than treat the entire generation path uniformly.
icml-2026-stable-velocity-a-variance-per.tldr: Stable Velocity uses variance differences along flow-matching paths to improve training and accelerate sampling within the low-variance region.

paragraphs: Strong prediction on satellite images can come from visual correlations without capturing the structure of the physical system. This paper calls that gap the Perception–Physics Paradox. It argues that some perception-based out-of-distribution accuracy measures are therefore poor indicators of how useful a representation is for scientific understanding.

The authors introduce scientific alignment as an objective for representation learning and study one testable aspect through structural isomorphism. This requires latent representations to identify physical systems uniquely up to a linear reparameterization. The framework produces a hierarchy of necessary conditions and a probing protocol for assessing physical and causal interpretability.

To put the analysis into practice, the paper introduces TC-Bench, a global tropical-cyclone dataset with an automated construction pipeline. Its evaluation finds that current vision foundation models use visual shortcuts that fail in extreme regimes. These observations indicate that scientific alignment does not automatically follow from scaling visual models alone. The benchmark and theory jointly shift evaluation toward whether learned representations preserve physically meaningful structure.
icml-2026-the-perceptionphysics-paradox-.tldr: TC-Bench probes whether visual representations preserve physical structure and finds shortcuts in current models that fail under extreme conditions.

paragraphs: Generating attractive music and convincing dance video does not ensure that the movement follows the music. Rhythm, phrasing, and accents need to connect with choreography at precise moments. TMD-Bench addresses this evaluation gap, which separate audio or video quality scores and generic audiovisual consistency measures do not adequately capture.

The benchmark evaluates text-driven music–dance generation along three dimensions: quality within each medium, adherence to instructions, and rhythmic alignment across music and motion. It combines computable physical measures with perceptual multimodal judgments. A curated dataset of rhythm-aligned music and dance supports the benchmark, alongside a Music Captioner that produces structured descriptions of musical meaning.

The evaluation finds that commercial audiovisual models such as Veo 3 and Sora 2 produce high-quality outputs while optimizing rhythmic coupling less consistently. The authors' unified baseline, RhyJAM, trained on rhythm-aligned data, achieves competitive beat synchronization and competitive quality in each medium. These findings highlight rhythmic coordination as a distinct target for both evaluation and model development.
icml-2026-tmd-bench-a-multi-level-evalua.tldr: TMD-Bench evaluates whether jointly generated music and dance follow instructions, look and sound good, and synchronize rhythmically.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts language models offer substantial expressive power but require enough memory to make deployment on constrained devices difficult. ZipMoE tackles this serving problem while preserving model behavior, using lossless compression rather than relying on lossy quantization. The goal is to make existing MoE models more practical to run locally.

The system jointly designs caching and scheduling around edge-device hardware and statistical redundancy in model parameters. Its design includes a provable performance guarantee. By coordinating how parameters are retained and work is scheduled, ZipMoE shifts inference away from an input/output bottleneck toward a computation-centered workflow that supports efficient parallel execution.

The authors implement a prototype and evaluate it on representative edge platforms with popular open-source MoE models and real workloads. They report up to 72.77% lower inference latency and up to 6.76 times higher throughput than state-of-the-art systems. These are best reported improvements, rather than uniform gains across all settings. The findings demonstrate the potential of coordinated compression, caching, and scheduling for behavior-preserving on-device inference.
icml-2026-zipmoe-efficient-on-device-moe.tldr: ZipMoE combines lossless compression with coordinated caching and scheduling to accelerate on-device MoE inference while preserving model behavior.
